Back in the day, (a couple decades ago) this was a game I enjoyed playing for hours. However, that was then. The years have not been kind to BG OG. Hence EE. But even the EE leaves some things to be desired and meanwhile I'd almost completely forgotten everything there is to know about the game except the antagonist's name and the trivial beginning stuff. Everything else is as if I'd never played it before. (Ah the sorrows/joys of getting old.) 

Pros: 
-- Story. This is why you buy the game. There is little in modern gaming that matches BG. Sadly, the IP has been copied over and over again in other games so some of the things that were unique to BG may seem trite or overplayed if you are a veteran RPG player and somehow never played this series.

-- Dungeons & Dragons. The game adheres very strictly to 2nd ed aD&D and that is not all a bad thing. For those who are fans of the system it means you already know much of how everything should work. (Except see the cons.)

-- Minsc & Boo. Of the VO actors this one is the best of the bunch. Set the bar for every game since imho. 

-- the EE DLC are actually quite a bit of value. Getting the BGEE with the dlc as part of a package deal is well worth the price of admission. 

-- the price of admission for me was very low at $20 for BG1 & 2, + Ice wind Dale with DLCs included. This seems like what a good sale should be like. If you have a chance at this, grab it.

-- my cds no longer are valid for my machine so this is really the only way I can play this game. This is a major reason why EE is a good thing. 


Cons
-- 2nd Edition aD&D. 1st Edition was more unforgiving in many ways but it was also less so because TSR had not figured out how to make a both accessible to mainstream players and good for old school gamers version of the game. So 2nd has some of the awkwardness and lack of balance of 1st edition but erred more on the side of not fun rather than over powered. So you will find combat to be hard and unforgiving. Be tactical at all times, because otherwise you will be reloading a lot. You will reload often anyway and you should save often anyway.

-- 2nd Edition characters suck in some not great ways. Multiclassing/experience gain in general is not well balanced and the pacing of the game is super slow so this makes it even worse. Be patient. Don't let the fact that you are 3 hours into the game and still working on getting to 2nd level in some of your characters bother you. Tis the nature of the game. 

-- Dying in BG is klunky and painful. Not because you lose anything per se. But because to keep from losing anything you have to pick up your fallen companion's gear and cart it with you. That's if your main character does not die. If that happens you will have to reload from a prior save. (Save often!) Thankfully the getting a dead person back part is not hard. You just have to manage to hike to a friendly temple and get the clergy to cast Raise Dead on them. For a fee which scales with your level. This is where a lot of your gold will go until you figure out how to keep alive in the tough fights.

-- The UI is Klunky and Painful. Yes that's right. Old games have klunky and painful UIs and the EE version did not do much to ameliorate that. (Though there are a EE couple work arounds that help. (cf: the reveal items button on the side above the gather party button and the red diamond button in the party interface that shows items on the ground nearby. So you don't have to strain your eyes looking for the hints against the background.

-- Merchants are annoying and the reputation/charisma based system does not help. The reason they are annoying is a mixed blessing as I think it does add to immersion that your blacksmith does not want your extra scrolls and the clergy may not want anything you have. But the roleplay aspects aside this is incredibly inconvenient because of the very limited inventory space each character gets. 

-- Inventory is limited to 16 slots plus what you can equip. This means a lot of fiddling and management and aching over what to keep and what to toss. What is worth the gp to drag back to town, etc. Which is also I suppose a good thing if your enjoyment is gained from making such decisions. For me it just blurs into the many other games with terrible inventory systems. 

-- Fights scale from hard to incredibly difficult as the game progresses. You will want auto pause on for almost everything. Without it you are at the mercy of a fast cpu making lightning quick moves while you are still adjusting to the fallout from prior moves. Be prepared to pause manually as well because some aspects of combat should not be left to chance. (Which spell your caster chooses next and which targets they choose for example.)

Now I haven't tried the easier modes of game play so maybe this isn't so bad in those but imho it is a hard adjustment to make. Don't be ashamed of lowering the difficulty if you find the game too frustrating. The higher settings are for challenges not to make you want to bust up your equipment. 

TLDR; Good old game with some serious flaws. Some are addressed by EE but not all and you may be best served by waiting for a sale.

[i]Baldur’s Gate[/i] is the role-playing game that set the standard for fantasy RPGs for decades, and if one were to compare its status and importance to works within cinema, it could fairly be called the [i]Citizen Kane[/i] of role-playing games. That is how significant and influential [i]BioWare[/i]’s 1998 classic truly is.

From a gameplay perspective, it feels close to perfection, even if younger players may initially find parts of it dated. However, if they give the game a genuine chance, I am convinced they will discover its greatness — especially thanks to the excellent “Enhanced Edition” releases by [i]Overhaul Games[/i]. The controls remain intuitive, and with the enormous flexibility surrounding difficulty options, the game is perfectly suited for both hardcore veterans and complete newcomers.

The game’s mise-en-scène is genuinely genre-defining, filled with varied and memorable environments. Personal highlights include the forests surrounding the Wood of Sharp Teeth. The colours of the trees still strike me during every playthrough as absolutely stunning. The world feels cohesive and alive, and the way characters react to your actions creates an impressive sense of immersion — especially for those who experienced the game in the late 1990s.

The dialogue is also of the highest quality, with a sense of humour that was never fully recaptured in [i]Siege of Dragonspear[/i], even if I still appreciate that expansion greatly, and perhaps above all for its ambition. The tone balances the deep darkness at the heart of the narrative with the adventurous spirit that defines most of the player’s journey. The pacing suits me perfectly as well, with a mystery that slowly grows larger and more ominous the longer you play, before culminating in a grand finale.

I have completed this game at least fifty times, and I will continue returning to this legendary adventure — especially in its refined Enhanced Edition form. In truth, I can barely mention a single negative aspect, simply because I am far too much of a fan, even if I fully understand why certain elements may frustrate some players. I loved the game when it released shortly before the turn of the millennium, and somehow, I love it even more today.

If you have the time, and are willing to invest yourself in a truly extraordinary role-playing game, then this is the ultimate place to begin.

Age may have formed a few cracks in its legendary skin, and perhaps the over reliance on randomness from the Dungeons and Dragons’ ruleset seems rather archaic, but within this slumbering ancient beast lies a mighty heart waiting to be awakened once more.

-inventory and character management is tiresome and a waste of too much time,

-why are there no spell range/AOE indicators (what the fuck does 50 ft. of range mean)?

-why must my whole party stop what they were ordered every time I order my party leader to speak with someone/investigate something...

Heck, [b] I don't even need quality of life and modern day UI and UX philosophies that much [/b] - bro I've played Path of Exile for 1.500 hours and I've played a decent amount of Warframe as well, do you really think I'm not used to an absolute pisspoor user experience - and yet still [b] Baldur's Gate feels even worse when trying to get into it than those games. This game is for people that either played it when it first came out or played other games at that time and are somewhat used to this level of clunkyness and weirdness - I may be playing old school games my whole life, but I was still born in the year 2000 - I've experienced too much quality of life to be comfortable playing this.

Maybe it's just not for me - that is always a possibility, we're all humans, we can't be good at everything and love everything.

Baldur’s Gate is one of the megaliths of the genre, but it does not reward being approached without nostalgia goggles. Coming to it without a childhood attachment, many of the details that long-time fans find charming read as bluntly hostile to modern sensibilities. This was [i]not[/i] a comforting return to the home country; it was a reminder of how uncompromising early cRPGs could be.

It [i]did[/i] impress with how it handled player agency. The world map was dotted with imposing locations left deliberately unexplained and ungated. You wandered into danger when you chose to; not when the story permitted. Where modern RPGs tend to apologise for their constraints, Baldur’s Gate offered none, and that confidence remains distinctive even now.

The enhanced edition did the work it needed to. The game was still ugly…but playable. I was never fooled into thinking I was playing something contemporary, but I could engage with it without fighting the interface. The achievement set was also unusually strong; varied and demanding, deeply integrated, and encouraging the exploration of systems and content, rather than rote grinding.

The weakest element was character class design. Old D&D rules bear much of the blame, but not of it; the re-release made little effort to clarify or mitigate the inherited problems. Multiclassing and dual-classing were poorly explained and inconsistently applied. Optimising your composition required hyperspecific memorisation, and the learning curve was quite steep.

Technical issues also surfaced. The addition of a console was welcome in theory, but I had to use it to bypass broken quest logic. The final boss encounter was wildly overtuned, tipping from climactic into excessive, but there’s that ‘faithful re-release’ necessity at play again, so I suppose that must be forgiven.

There were also some, shall we say, ‘out-of-game’ issues. Beamdog’s habit of directly responding to negative Steam reviews felt defensive and unnecessary. These were subjective impressions from genre fans, not press crises…

In the end, the recommendation was and is conditional but firm. If “classic fantasy isometric RPG” already holds appeal, or if achievement hunting is part of the draw, Baldur’s Gate: Enhanced Edition remains worth the effort. For everyone else, its historical importance may outweigh its entertainment value.

I'll be writing this review mainly directed to people who don't really know much about Dungeons & Dragons or old-school cRPG's.

One of the first games to have branching story paths that actually worked and meant something. Lots of consequence, lots of choices, lots of endings. 

The story of the game is very well written and also interesting. If you're willing to read up on the background information a little to get a grasp of what the D&D world is like, particuarly this one, then you'll understand the games story better. Even if you don't read any background information you'll still pick up on it as you play, and you'll still be able to enjoy it.

The first few hours of the game are a little slow and sort of random. During these few hours (about 2-3 hours or so), lots of random things will be thrown at you just to let you practice on how the game works. You'll meet random companions, random attacks, and have some pretty pointless but rewarding side quests. Like I said, these are just to warm you up on the rest of the game.

One of the main points of the game is maintaining a party. You'll meet many companions along your adventure which you can either allow into your party or not. You must watch each players health, weapons, stats, and so on. It sounds complicated when you first read about it, but it's pretty easy once you get used to it. Your companions will get tired, get wounded or their weapons will break. You have to watch out for all of these things and help them out as much as you can. Fortunately for people who have a hard time making characters, you will only have to make your own character (which is the leader of the party) as all other companions will have their own stats and abilities. With that being said, you must know how to use and level up their stats and abilities.

The combat can be a bit tricky at first, especially once your party gets pretty large. You are able to pause the game, point out each individual party member who to attack, then unpause. Having your whole party attack the same enemy at once works on lower level enemies, but as you start to face larger groups of monster and/or more challenging enemies, you have to use strategy to determine how not to get your party instantly killed.

The character creation is quite big for this game. You can chose between a few races, pick between many classes which have their own sub-classes (Such has Cleric/Ranger or Cleric/Thief, etc.) and have quite a bit of stats to level up. You won't be leveling up as easily or quickly as many of todays RPGs. I didn't upgrade my main character until about 2 hours into the game while doing a bunch of side-quests and killing lots of enemies. Leveling up is meant to feel rewarding and having an actual impact when adding points to stats and gaining new abilites.

The world is nicely drawn in this game too. The graphics on the Enhanced Version doesn't look much better than when I played this game years ago, but at least it's in widescreen.

Exploring the world is also a huge point in this game. The world isn't all one seamless level, but instead it's broken up into large sections which usually have other sections within them, such as caves and castles. Most of the places you're allowed to freely enter, but others are restricted.

I guess there's also multiplayer, but I guess i'm the only one in my friends list that owns this game haha.

Overall, I think this game is very good, and the Enchanced Edition brings some changes that will ease in newcomers to the classing cRPG genre. This is considered by many to be one of the best RPG games to date, as well as the other D&D cRPG's that came out around the same time. I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of RPGs and are willing to overcome a slight learning curve if they haven't played a classic cRPG such as this before.

Your party should include at least a Cleric, a Wizard, a frontline fighter, and someone with thief skills. Most of these roles can be multiclassed if necessary (a Cleric/Mage is fine, for example.)
Don't hoard your consumables, use them whenever things get rough.
The Golden Pantaloons can be carried over to the sequel and doing so while also finding and holding on to that game's set of Pantaloons will eventually net you an interesting reward in the sequel's expansion.

Character Stats

Attributes: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma. Most attributes are very top-heavy, 17/18 is where they start having real impact while the difference between 10 and 14 is minimal.
Armor Class: Lower is better, 10 is the worst. Your defence against physical attacks that's based off your Dexterity bonus, armor, shield and any magic protective spells/equipment.
THAC0: Lower is better, 20 is the worst. Your attack rating, equal to the number you need to roll on a 20-sided die to hit 0 Armor Class.
Saving Throws: Lower is better. Your non-physical defenses against magic attacks, poison, etc. To succeed at a save, you need to roll equal to or above your Saving Throw value on a 20-sided die.

Absolute classic. In which way?
Let's take Dracula by Bram Stoker for example. Absolute horror classic that layed the basis of every single vampire story that came after. Does it mean it was one of a kind? Not really... Other vampire books were written before (Carmilla), but it was this one that stuck to people. When you're reading Dracula, you can sense just how much it has influenced pop culture and literature for the next century and a half. 
Similarly, playing Baldurs Gate makes you recognise mechanics  that games 30 years after are still using. 
For example, the morale system. It wasn't the first one to use it, mind you, but the impact it has on some interactions is definetly groundbreaking, and so is the pacing of the story. 
You never feel like you're dragging or digressing when you're completing a side-quest, for two reasons. First, the quality of the side material is just as good as the main story, so you're not feeling the abrupt downgrade in writing quality that characterizes "filler episodes" in TV or literature. Secondly, sometimes they're written into the story so well that you don't realize you're sidequesting. You're gonna run into a town in your travels that tell you of a super powered magic tower, and your journal (absoltue banger mechanic that let's you organically keep track of everything that's happened) tells you it'll be important. In that same town you have a passage to a dungeon, and a mission about freeing the naive halfling residents of the town from a underground secret cult that kidnaps their people in the night (you can even help the organization and kidnap the kids yourself!!). All of this happens in a throwaway town in the middle of nowhere that you just... run into. And you're compelled to explore it because the main story organically incorporates the town in the journey, and doesn't pressure the player into completing it, instead it just points into a direction, letting you craft your own adventure as you see fit. 
Sound familiar? Fallout New Vegas, the critically overlooked-fan favourite-cult object- incomplete masterpiece of a game, uses an identical format in their narrative, twelve years after the release of BG1.
It is also crucial to talk about other aspects of the game like the visual design (I've only played the Enhanced edition), killer soundtrack, amazing sound design, and the companion system. I've heard this last one was kind of an afterthought...? It's amazing nonetheless, and a fucking [i] statement [/i] about how to make a rag-tag gang of adventurers feel like real people with [i] so little dialogue [/i]. They interact with each other and have their own personality outside of the player's choice: they complain, laugh and critisize the player's decisions, and will leave your party if you do something they didn't like. The way a character is so fundamentally linked to another (because they're married/are best friends/etc), that you need to have them both or neither in your party is a testament of how to design a character with practically no tools. 
Like cinema, gaming used to be an art of "smoke and mirrors", where they used certain mechanics, visual or sound cues to make the player feel something or understand something without explicity showing it. Also like cinema, in recent years the capital game developers and distribuitors are willing to invest in a project has grown astronomically. That increase in budget, in RPGs, has been translated into companion NPCs having fully animated, expresive bodies and faces that express their personalities, but more often than not they lack the dramatic or narrative basis that makes a compelling character. The problem has been shifted from the 90s: then, it was compelling characters made of smoke and mirrors, now, they're very pretty animatronics with nothing inside 'em. Companions nowadays [i] make [/i] the game. Just take a look at Youtube Channels like Fluffyninjallama, that based their entire career into showing you different reactions companions have to your choices  or random banter in games like Mass Effect, Fallout 4, or the recent masterpiece that is Baldurs Gate 3. 
I loved Baldurs Gate 1, but I would only recommend it to people who are willing to spend time and sweat into understanding the game and playing by its rules. Not to say it's clunky (it is), but rather demanding. You need to understand its complicated, unexplained, bulls**t 90's Dungeons and Dragons mechanics to play the game (or you can play in story mode difficulty, completely valid). I don't wish to drag too much on this, but I love when a game forces you to master it, rather than rounden up its edges to result in an insipid experience. When a game has tact, taste and its own characteristic flavour, you develop a special relationship (stockholm syndrom, that is) with it, imbuing itself in your brain.
Before playing this game, I'd recommend a new player to experience newer Classic RPGs (CRPGs) like Divinity 2, Baldurs Gate 3 or even Dragon Age Origins. If you're interested in this game, playing the others will not make this one feel like such a big step. 

Best case scenario, you're left craving for more. Worst, you're filtered off. 
Just don't start by IceWind Dale like my poor cousin did, got it?

You will find no quest waypoints and very little in the way of statistic or spell explanations, meaning you will have to have patience learning and understanding the obviously outdated mechanics.

[h1]Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition[/h1]

I just replayed the original Baldur's Gate over a few days. Why? Honestly, I’m not sure—I had a sudden urge to revisit a game I loved and beat as a kid but never fully understood mechanically. I figured I’d create a character (Half-elf Conjuror) and bounce off it after an hour or two, due to its age.

I was pleasantly surprised to find myself locked in for hours.

It’s kind of amazing how well this game holds up, considering it’s 27 years old (!). That says a lot about the staying power of the CRPG genre—and the quality of the original. The Enhanced Edition (2013) (“EE”) deserves credit here, too: it allows for modern resolutions and quality-of-life tweaks that make a big difference. The hand-painted backdrops and stylized sprites still look charming enough that the dated visuals never pulled me out of the experience.

I’ve always had fond memories of the characters—Minsc, Jaheira, Imoen—but I was surprised by how little dialogue or interaction they actually have in the first game. Most companions have 2–3 lines and then more or less fade into the background.

Still, they’re strong archetypes, and their personalities come through clearly from their introductions. I realized that a lot of my emotional connection to them comes from Baldur’s Gate II, which gives them far more depth. However, their presence here is still meaningful, especially if you’re planning to move on to the sequel.

Gameplay is where the experience really clicked for me. I remember the game being tough back in the day—but this time, playing on Core Rules, I found it quite manageable. Understanding the AD&D ruleset and knowing how to build a party made a huge difference. It’s extremely satisfying to use the right buffs, counters, and spell combinations at the right time.

That said, it’s a slow burn. Early levels can feel restrictive—my Conjuror could only slightly contribute to most fights until I hit level 5. But once I had access to level 3 spells and the Ring of Wizardry, everything opened up. With a solid party (Dynaheir, Jaheira, and others), I could buff, debuff, and nuke with confidence. From that point on, combat felt genuinely rewarding.

Tip: The game runs slowly by default. You can edit the .ini file to raise the framerate cap from 30 to 45 or 60 FPS—it makes a huge difference in pacing and responsiveness.

The Enhanced Edition adds new companions and the Siege of Dragonspear expansion (released in 2016 by Beamdog, not Bioware) that bridges the story between BG1 and BG2. I tried the new companions when EE launched and they never quite fit—they felt tonally off compared to the originals. So I skipped them this time.

As for Siege of Dragonspear, it kicks in right after the final cutscene of BG1. I gave it about an hour, but I had the same reaction—something about the writing and atmosphere didn’t feel quite right, so I’d rather move on to Baldur’s Gate II. Maybe it’s just me, but it lacked the charm of the original. I always felt that the story didn’t need “bridging” between BG1 and BG2. 

Was this playthrough nostalgia-fueled? Probably. But it was also fun—about 45 hours of it. Baldur’s Gate remains a landmark title, and even with its slower early game and some light companion content, it still delivers a rich, strategic, and surprisingly immersive experience.

If you're a fan of isometric RPGs, tactical combat, or D&D-style systems, this game is absolutely worth a visit. Just be patient at the start, tweak the framerate, and embrace the magic.

Baldur's Gate Enhanced Edition is a good cRPG that's worth playing. Yet simultaneously parts of it have not aged well, despite the Enhanced Edition, and will turn some players off.

In comparison to more modern cRPGs, Baldur's Gate is very freeform in how you can approach things. The story is there, largely well-written, and frequently referenced, but for most of the game you're free to go and explore anywhere you wish. You can kill just about anyone you meet, or help them out of course. And there are something like 20-30 potential party members, so that no matter what alignment you end up on you can always have a useful party along for the ride.

The 2nd edition D&D rules the game is based on are quite archaic, but do offer a huge amount of variety. There are a lot of classes and sub-types to play around with in addition to dual- or multi-classing. A fair few races with different bonuses. A bunch of stats (although charisma/intellect/wisdom largely don't do much). Loads of different weapon types. Absurd amounts of spells, scrolls, potions, etc. It genuinely feels like a D&D adventure in game format, especially at the start with all the exploration.

The quests, exploration, and story are the highlights. Though this game is story-light compared to something like Planescape Torment, what's there is still very interesting and sets things up for some real strong potential in Baldur's Gate 2. It's an all-around good game. And if you can suffer its shortcomings, well worth a playthrough.

There are those shortcomings though...

Baldur's Gate 1 most clearly shows its age with pathfinding. It's atrocious. Wanna see party members banging their heads against each other for 5 minutes straight, no matter how often you click for them to move apart? You can, in this game. It's infuriating when it happens, but also not an insurmountable problem. Party AI in general is also very rudimentary, but that can also be said for more modern games like Pillars of Eternity...

Similarly the user interface leaves a lot to be desired. Only being able to quick-slot 3 items and 3 spells? One of the most obnoxiously limited and clearly dated inventory systems in the RPG genre? Sure, Diablo 1's is MUCH worse, but that's literally as low as that bar can actually go. A UI that on a 21:9 by monitor can only be toggled between "you-must-be-blind" and "please-wear-a-telescope" sizes. This on top of everything important being communicated in a dialogue screen with oversized text. Wanna know what that enemy mage cast, or whether you're even hitting your enemy with basic attacks, or whether your spell even did anything? Scroll through the lines in that dialogue screen...

The game only runs at 30 fps, because gameplay logic is tied to that frame rate, which turns into an absolute stutterfest when panning the camera. The environment design is generally very simplistic. The end was clearly rushed as the environment design is largely atrocious, the encounter design even more all over the place than the rest of the game, and the quests barely there at all. The writing at the end was good and definitely made me interested in BG2 though...

As mentioned, the encounter design is all over the place, which is common in cRPGs. Surprisingly I thought BGEE was actually mostly... too easy. On Core Rules difficulty. Get some magical (+1) weapons and ammo the moment you can afford it and there goes your level 1-2 party demolishing most level 6 groups trivially. There are some hard encounters, even brutal ones that subvert the game mechanics, but they're few and far between. Mostly either at the very uneven end, or in the Tales of the Sword Coast expansion content. And even those were far easier to deal with than the nastier fights in Pillars of Eternity 1 & 2. This was a bit of a problem as the endless easy fights combined with slow walking speed pre-Haste-spell meant the middle of the game dragged. It didn't drag nearly as much as PoE though, and only for a while. Haste fixes things nicely!

There is some more archaic design holding the game back, like no respecs. An issue if you put proficiency points into the wrong weapons, or you're a sorceror and picked the wrong spell. Saving a lot helps. On that note, the quick save system with multiple rotating slots is actually much more convenient than in most modern cRPGs!

The writing, while overall quite good, is a bit shaky. It doesn't have the same tone throughout, even if you ignore Beamdog's anachronous additions. Some areas of the game are much more fleshed out than others. And the end of the game is very rushed in encounter and environment design, although the story is quite compelling at that point.

With the right perspective there is a lot of fun to be had here, even for a newcomer in 2023. I had a great time playing through BGEE and the ending made me look forward to booting up BG2. I suspect that game will truly live up to the classic status, with what's been set up here, while I think BGEE is more just a great game held back by a lot of minor annoyances and it being the first RPG of its kind for BioWare. Planescape Torment is a big step above for me, although that game is more story-heavy where this is gameplay-focused.

If you think you have what it takes to look past the annoyances to the gem underneath... pick this up and give it a go. You might just have a really great time with it.

There is so much I left on the table here. Def wanted to get through the series ahead of Baldur’s Gate 3 August release. For a game this old, I’m honestly blown away at how good this story is. In a genre filled with “the end is nigh” storytelling, it’s great to see a really grounded story. 

Game does very little to help you understand the mechanics operating in the background, but you can stumble your way through, as I have.

If you like D&D and understand how this version of D&D works, this is a must play game. With that being said, if you are not ready to strap yourself in for some BS (if you play a wizard it makes so much of the game easier imo) I would probably just wait until BG3 or play more modern games like Divinity. The combat system will throw some silly fights at you and if you are not ready, there will be some headaches. 

The music is great, the characters are great, combat is mostly great if you play it turn by turn, and the choices you make really feels like you are making meaningful choices in this world. The overall story is pretty cookie cutter, but for a game this old, it probably felt more fresh back then than it does nowadays. 

Overall, is the game worth picking up at full price? Yes! You can easily dump 60+ hours into this game and it is regularly on sale for under $10.

Baldur’s Gate is one of the best simulations of the AD&D 2e experience. This is both a compliment and an insult. Ultimately, I think this is a good game and worth playing if you can get over a lot of the dated game design. But if you’re a total newcomer to CRPGs, especially those of the late 90s, this game is a trial by fire. I would not recommend this game to anyone who simply wants to play it for the story, because on top of it being just okay, this game’s strength is the way you interact with the world more so than it is the quality of the narrative itself and that means getting deep into the mechanics of the game.

To start positively, Baldur’s Gate is great at presenting the Forgotten Realms D&D setting. If you’re a lore nerd, there is a lot to dive into here. There are countless books explaining the history of the region, its gods, and the politics of the kingdoms hidden all over the place. Bartenders will tell you rumors if you buy drinks from them, and each powerful magical item has a story in its description. There is a decent amount of environmental storytelling in the maps as well, moreso in the Tales of the Sword Coast expansion pack than the base game, which are beautiful and colorful and look like you’re playing in a painting. It’s a unique feel of 2D and 2.5D isometric sprite games like this can provide that you just can’t get from a photorealistic 3D rendering. Unfortunately, the character models on the other hand range from okay to “what the fuck am I looking at?” and the lack of a unique visual profile on most of the humanoid sprites makes it tough to pick out important targets like spellcasters when the combat starts.

The plot of Baldur’s Gate is fine. It’s a pretty bog-standard D&D adventure of discovering an evil bad guy’s plot to take over a kingdom and eventually saving it. There is a bit of interesting in-game politics that sets the backdrop for the campaign and ties into the characters, but it’s not by any means some deep or thoughtful narrative. The real strength of the story comes from how you can interact with it via choices made in dialogue, combat, party composition, etc. Outcomes of major plot points aren’t going to change, but side quests can be much more open ended by simply having the right (or wrong) companion in your party. And the side quests are so numerous and wide in scope that many of them will have direct connections to the main quest, even if they aren’t necessary to progress. Combine that with the sheer amount of companions in this game (29 in total) and the way they interact with each other while in the party, and there is simply no way to see it all in a single playthrough.

The only real issue I have with the narrative, outside of it just stopping instead of having a proper ending, is that its pacing is crippled by the side quests and gameplay in general. There is a calendar in the game keeping track of the time you have spent on your adventure, but it is never important outside of certain companion’s quests. The big bad evil guy will always be about to reach his goal, no matter if it takes you 2 in-game days or 2 in-game months to find him; and you will be spending months preparing for that next step. Following the main quest alone will leave you severely underleveled and you have to grind side quests, which is time consuming both in-game and in person. Healing and recovering spells means resting for at least 8 hours at a time. And if you don’t have many healing potions or spells, that means you could be spending literal in-game weeks trudging through a dungeon. All of this makes it almost impossible to avoid ruining the pacing. Maybe it’s a testament to everything else that I find this is immersion breaking, but it is nonetheless.

The reason you will have to do some grinding is that this game is HARD. Part of this is AD&D 2e’s design, but some of this is on the game too. Characters, especially early on, will have very little HP depending on the class. A martial focused class like a fighter might be able to take a hit or resist being hit in the first place, but god help your mages who can easily be killed by a single arrow until around lvl 5. And since combat plays out in real time, characters can be obliterated in the blink of an eye.

I don’t think it’s a bad thing that combat is this hard, even on easier difficulties. I do have a problem with it playing out in real time though. The pathing AI is atrocious, and the pace at which it plays out is fast. Thankfully you can pause combat and still choose actions and even set up auto-pause triggers for certain events, but it’s not easy to get the hang of nor all that satisfying once mastered. I never felt like any of my successful battles were a result of my immediate tactical decisions like it would in a game like Xcom, mostly because there isn’t much you can do while watching them play out. Most of the strategy has to come from knowing what you’re up against ahead of time and preparing before the actual fight.

AD&D 2e has this, quite frankly, terrible spell slot memorization mechanic in which every spellcaster must choose their spells for each available slot on a short rest. For example: if you have 3 lvl 1 slots and want to cast magic missile 3 times, then you had to have already memorized 3 magic missile spells during your last rest and you won’t be able to cast any other lvl spells that you’d know until you swap slots on the next rest. It forces you to plan ahead for encounters and dungeons, except there is no way of figuring out what to expect on your first playthrough so your best bet is to just Edge of Tomorrow your way through the game. This isn’t the only complaint I have about AD&D 2e either. In this system, the thief class is the only one capable of disarming traps (of which there are a lot in this game that are unavoidable and will only trigger for player controlled characters for some reason), mages can fail to learn spells from scrolls on a dice roll (which easier difficulties at least disables), THAC0 exists, the list of shit goes on. It’s an outdated and unnecessarily complicated system on its own, and translating it into a video game only serves to highlight its issues.

Then there’s the gameplay elements outside of the AD&D system. You know all those cool companions that you can form a party of 6 out of? Well you’re gonna have to remember where you left them because they are going to remain scattered across the world if you talk to them and decide to swap party members. Only a few of the Enhanced Edition characters will hang out at a central location. Companions not in your party are not getting experience points either, so you better be happy with your decision on who’s in the party and pray they survive. You’d think that the game wants you to replace dead characters based on how many there are, but I am not going to spend 30 hours grinding up a replacement when they are 7 levels behind. And I’m certainly not gonna waste my time trying to revive the dead because they don’t come back with their stuff, and I’m not about to spend 40 minutes trekking back and forth to get everything with how annoying this inventory system is; being that individual characters need their inventories managed separately. Some of this is easier to overlook than others, but I have to call it out because it’s clearly a problem that was fixed in future sequels and expansions.

Obviously, I wouldn’t say that all of these problems make the game unplayable; I’m still recommending the game after all. I do think it’s important to mention though because it’ll backhand slap any newcomer across the face and probably deter them from sticking with it. It almost kept me from doing so, until it finally clicked for me in the final chapter of the game. Perhaps on a replay, now that I know what I’m doing and what to expect, I will have a better experience. I just wish that better experience was something I could’ve gotten the first time.

After falling in love with BG3, wanted to give the originals/classics a go... and I am so incredibly glad I did. 

All the praise and high review ratings for this game are 1000% merited. 

This game is truly an experience that will most likely be memorable for your entire lifetime. I am not even kidding, this game even with its dated graphics/user interface... if you can get over that (which in my case was very quick) you are in for one hell of a Bhaalspawn ride. 

Not only is the core game beyond amazing... Siege of Dragonspear (SoD) expansion pack/add-on/DLC? Do NOT sleep or even dream of skipping it. SoD made one of the best isometric CPRG experiences even better. It really was the icing on top after an already astonishing experience. 

If you are still hesitant on pulling the trigger for this classic and you are reading this - the time is now. No more waiting. Take the plunge. You will not regret it.

I do still recommend this game after the changes.
Were they horribly unneeded and spat on a classic? Yes.
So why do I still recommend it?

Because, if you go to the beta opting for the game, you can set the game to an older patch, 1.3 to be exact, which is before any of the unnecessary changes took place. So while yes, the update made the game far...far worse. I say EE is still the more stable version of the game as it stands for newer hardware and I'm happy to say that yes, you can infact, avoid that atrocious and unneeded update. If you still want to give them money or not is up to you, I honestly say they don't deserve it but the game itself is still worth it.

Just so people stop freaking out as if there is no way to change everything back, I hope this helps some of you that planned on buying the game and were put off or people who already bought the game and were pretty pissed!

Although I will say the Multiplayer side of the game is pretty buggy, for both this and the second game. Not really sure why, but the connecting players tend to crash when loading new zones. It's best to get the original game if you want to use the multiplayer aspect.

To be fair, while the graphics and gameplay are ludicrously ancient, there is a very large and engrossing story to follow, a couple dozen interesting companions, and a well-realized world. The character builds are huge in variety (but woe unto those who don't know how to build properly), leading to a wide array of options. Because of its age, I can only recommend this game to those with incredible patience--it's text heavy, you move very slowly and the AI pathfinding is abysmal. I won't give it a score...it's not appropriate for such an old game with a specific audience.

Took me years to fully appreciate, especially growing up with games like skyrim and the like. But now that I took the time to understand it's a different experience and learn how it played, it became really fun. Trust me, once you get past all the classic crpg stuff that you aren't used to, it's a really good game.

It took me a bit to get accustom to the old graphics and feel of the game--and damn the movement of the characters and camera feel rough--but once it did, I can tell why this game is regarded as a classic. I had spent all of my time doing side content and when I finally reached the Nashkel mines, I was rocking a level 6 party. The interactions with some of the NPCs are surprisingly hilarious in this game, and I enjoy the companion system quite a bit.

Still playing through the game, but I would definitely recommend. Can't wait to get to BGII and then BGIII when it comes out.

Oldest RPG I have ever played. There is bunch of content here, but at same time you can feel old age in this game. Would say that it has aged as gracefully as it can, but there things sticking out as a sore thumb.
Used program to roll stats (human paladin), Core Rules difficulty, played with full party (mostly didnt cheese), did Tales Of The Sword Coast expansion (didnt do Black Pits or newest DLC), use of wiki was limited (mostly for checking which companions should pick).
Will continue with Baldurs Gate 2.

PROS:
+ Bunch of spells to learn and use
+ Can play solo or in party
+ Bunch of items to find and exploit/sell
+ Interesting quests/encounters (many interesting moments)
+ The land and Baldurs Gate feels big
+ Dungeon design is very good
+ Combat generally is challenging (as long as you dont cheese or arent going to a lot lower level zones - there isnt any kind of enemy scaling in the game)
+ Feels rewarding to master the system (still feel as beginner, even though managed to beat the game)

CONS:
- No bank, mostly store spare equipment in barrels/boxes
- Graphics (the quality is the problem not aesthetics/style, but this is an old game)
- Easy to miss content (need to check all nooks and crannies)
- You will die a lot
- Incompatible companions will kill each other or leave party
- Too high or low reputation will make specific companions leave
- Disbanding companion most of the time will make them stay in the same place (RIP Faldron, your fault for not running out of flooded mine)
- No indicator for size of AOE spells/effects
- Movement for full party can be clunky (blocking each others movement)

+/- Bunch of companions (some come in pairs), basically impossible to see everything in one playthrough
+/- If you know then many ways how to cheese system

Summary:
If you dont have any more modern RPG you want to play OR if you want to know from where many modern RPG game decision took place (or at least got inspired from) OR if you just a big DnD fan (who is interested in older systems) then I suggest this game. Game is solid, but you can feel age on it.

Will Rate:
You must gather your party before venturing forth out of 10

A definite and significant improvement on the original series.  If this was your jam back in the day, take a stroll down memory lane.  If you didnt grow up in the isometric age, you'll probably hate it unless you are into D&D.

I've been playing this game (or a version of it) off and on since 1998.  It and its sequal BG2 are such good games mechanically, with such a responsive engine, that it's still my favorite implementation of the D&D rules (2nd edition/Advanced in this case) in any PC game.  On top of that, the story across these two games are incredible.  Yes, the character interactions are a bit weak in this, the first of the Bioware games, but a lot of the ground work that appears later is started here.  And better, of all the Infinity Engine games I've played, this one most encapsulates that feeling of wonder and terror that is low-level, old school D&D.  

Highly recommend this game.
